stimulus.body: Cartographer's projection #4060 reads: Er hilft dem Team. The verb governs a dative object.

questions.stem: Which case does 'helfen' govern in this sentence?
questions.explanation: 'Helfen' governs dative case. The object appears in dative, not accusative.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Two objects and the order they take
questions.learningObjective: Order two objects when one is a pronoun
questions.stem: In cartographer's projection #4274 the sentence 'Ich gebe es dem Mann' has a pronoun object. Which object comes first?

options.text: The dative pronoun comes first always.
The dative noun 'dem Mann' comes first.
Both objects come after the verb only.

questions.explanation: When the accusative object is a pronoun, it precedes the dative object. This is an exception to the standard rule.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A word order question decided by the verb
questions.learningObjective: Explain transitive versus intransitive verb pairs
questions.stem: Explain the difference between transitive and intransitive verb pairs like 'stellen' and 'stehen'.

answer.exemplar: 'Stellen' is transitive and takes an accusative object, while 'stehen' is intransitive and takes none; the verb determines the case pattern.

questions.explanation: The verb's valency determines whether an accusative object is possible. Transitive verbs require one; intransitive verbs do not.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A sentence-final verb in a question
questions.learningObjective: Use verb-final order in an indirect question

stimulus.body: Cartographer's projection #4374 reads: Ich frage, ob er kommt. The clause is an indirect question.

questions.stem: Where does the finite verb stand in this indirect question?

options.text: It stands at the end of the clause.
It stands after the object only.

questions.explanation: An indirect question is a subordinate clause, so the finite verb stands at the end. Main-clause order would be wrong.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: An elliptical question
questions.learningObjective: Identify an elliptical question in a text
questions.stem: Cartographer's projection #4481 stage one asks whether 'Und das soll ich glauben?' is elliptical; stage two asks what is omitted. What is the stage-one answer?

options.text: No, it is a complete question.
Yes, it is an elliptical question.
No, it is an indirect question.

questions.explanation: An elliptical question omits understood elements. The implied subject and verb are recovered from context.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A reflexive pronoun and its case
questions.learningObjective: Use the dative reflexive pronoun correctly
questions.stem: In cartographer's projection #4588 the sentence 'Ich wasche mir die Hände' uses a reflexive pronoun. What case is 'mir'?
questions.explanation: When a separate accusative object is present, the reflexive pronoun takes dative case. 'Mir' is the first-person dative form.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A dative object and a case-sensitive verb
questions.learningObjective: Explain which verbs take a dative object
questions.stem: Explain which German verbs require a dative object instead of an accusative one.

answer.exemplar: Verbs like 'helfen', 'danken', and 'glauben' govern a dative object, so the noun appears in dative case.

questions.explanation: These verbs select dative case for their object. The accusative would be ungrammatical with such verbs.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Two objects and the order they take
questions.learningObjective: Order two objects in standard position
questions.stem: Cartographer's projection #4802 stage one asks for the order of dative and accusative objects; stage two asks about pronoun exceptions. What is the stage-one order?

options.text: Place both objects after the verb only.
Place the accusative object before the dative object.
Place the dative object before the accusative object.
Place the accusative object first always.

questions.explanation: In standard order, the dative object precedes the accusative object. The pronoun exception is a separate rule.
